claims.quote: The only exceptions are for certain married couples filing a joint federal return in the following situations: • One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident. / In this case, you must either: – file separate New York returns using filing status ; or – file jointly, as if you both were New York State residents, using filing status .
claims.why_uncovered: The status item takes the federal filing status unchanged and cites only the general rule ("In most cases, you must use the same filing status you used on your federal return"). Nothing in the encoding covers the exception for a joint federal filer whose spouse is a nonresident or part-year resident of New York. No question asks about the spouses' residency, and no refusal covers the case. The HANDLED ELSEWHERE refusals are about federal filing-status tests and nonresident aliens for the EIC, so they do not cover it either. In this case New York requires married filing separately, or a joint return as if both spouses were residents, so the federal status cannot simply be carried over.

sentences.quote: If you received foreign income but did not receive a federal Form W-2, you must complete Form IT-2.

claims.quote: If you received foreign income but did not receive a federal Form W-2, you must complete Form IT-2.
claims.why_uncovered: The encoding produces one IT-2 record per Form W-2, and every question asks about amounts on a W-2. Nothing asks whether the filer had foreign income without a W-2, and nothing refuses that case. So the required IT-2 for that income is never produced.

claims.quote: Also enter the required information for any dependent you were entitled to claim on your federal return but chose not to (see Example below). / If you did not have to file a federal return, enter the required information for each dependent you would be entitled to claim for federal income tax purposes. / Note: If you are married filing a joint federal return but are required to file separate returns for New York State, complete item H as if you filed separate federal returns.
claims.why_uncovered: The item H count is drawn from the dependents on the federal return. No question asks whether a dependent the filer could have claimed federally, but chose not to claim (for example, so the child could take an education credit), should also be listed. No refusal covers that case either. The count feeds the line 36 exemption and the household-credit and IT-270 people counts.

claims.quote: If you are a New York City resident or part-year resident and you marked Yes at item C on the front of Form IT-201 indicating that you can be claimed as a dependent on another taxpayer’s federal return, or your income (see below) is more than $500,000, you do not qualify to claim this credit.
claims.why_uncovered: For line 69a the encoding only refuses when income is over $500,000 (gate.stc_rr_income). The item C test is encoded for line 69 (stc_fixed_eligible), but no listed gate or helper denies the rate reduction amount when item C is Yes.

claims.why_uncovered: The New York filing status is taken from the federal return. The only exception the encoding handles is a spouse who is a nonresident or part-year resident (gate.spouse_nonresident). Nothing asks about, or refuses, a federal joint filer who must or may file a separate New York return because the spouse cannot be found or refuses to sign. That changes the filing status, the standard deduction, the tax and the credits.

sentences.quote: Therefore, for any tax year of the marriage, a servicemember and their spouse may elect to use, for purposes of taxation, any of the following (regardless of the date they married): • the residence or domicile of the servicemember • the residence or domicile of the spouse • the permanent duty station of the servicemember

claims.quote: Therefore, for any tax year of the marriage, a servicemember and their spouse may elect to use, for purposes of taxation, any of the following (regardless of the date they married): • the residence or domicile of the servicemember • the residence or domicile of the spouse • the permanent duty station of the servicemember / Note: Special rules under the SCRA apply to members of the military and their spouses for determining residency.
claims.why_uncovered: The residency question asks only about domicile, the statutory 184-day test and Groups A/B, plus active duty for the 184-day test. Nothing asks about an SCRA residence election (codes M4–M9), especially by a civilian spouse. Such an election can make a filer a nonresident or change their residence. The special_code gate says the other codes are refused elsewhere, but no listed refusal covers the SCRA election.

claims.why_uncovered: The MCTMT question and the mctmt_possible helper rely on Schedule C profit and on the filer's own view of net earnings from self-employment. Neither tells the filer to count a 'limited partner' distributive share when the partner takes part in management. Neither tells the filer to count earnings that are not subject to federal SE tax. A filer in either situation could answer No and skip the MCTMT refusal.

claims.quote: The only exceptions are for certain married couples filing a joint federal return in the following situations: • One spouse is a New York State resident and the other is a nonresident or part-year resident. / In this case, you must either: – file separate New York returns using filing status ; or – file jointly, as if you both were New York State residents, using filing status .
claims.why_uncovered: The status item is bound directly to the federal filing status. It cites only the general rule ("In most cases, you must use the same filing status you used on your federal return"). Nothing asks whether one spouse on a joint federal return was a New York resident and the other a nonresident or part-year resident. Nothing refuses that case either. In that case New York requires either married filing separately (status ③, the single schedule) or a joint return as if both were residents (status ②). The encoding would just carry the federal joint status through to the married filing jointly schedule. No refusal on the HANDLED ELSEWHERE list covers this New York mixed-residency exception. The f1040 filing-status refusals only test federal marriage facts.
